extraction_notes: Exhaustive extraction of 24 core concepts spanning foundational instrumental interaction theory (Beaudouin-Lafon reification/polymorphism/reuse), post-WIMP paradigms, direct manipulation principles, AI-augmented extensions (AI-Instruments, Interaction-Augmented Instructions), cognitive foundations (embodied cognition, cognitive load, mental models), and supporting frameworks (reality-based interaction, information foraging). Coverage reflects the leaf's dual scope: classical instrumental interaction principles AND contemporary AI-Instruments applications. All concepts grounded in available sources (26 unique source_ids across the 24 concepts). Strength assessment: 7 established-law, 10 framework/hypothesis, 7 empirical. Fields distributed across HCI (primary), cognitive-psych, information-foraging, and visual-programming/interaction-design where relevant. Concepts interconnect to show how reification+polymorphism+reuse enable instrumental interaction, which extends to post-WIMP paradigms, and further to AI-augmented systems. Coverage addresses the MetroGraph wedge: surface-area bloat is addressed through reification/polymorphism/currying (fewer commands, more objects); flight to AI chat is addressed through Interaction-Augmented Instructions (combining prompts with visual manipulation); agent-vs-graph confusion is addressed through Reflection and Grounding principles showing users multiple interpretations before commitment. No sources invented; all citations map to sources.json id pool with T1 (peer-reviewed) sources prioritized.

concepts.definition: An interaction model where user actions are mediated by interaction instruments (tools) that act upon domain objects, extending direct manipulation principles to post-WIMP interfaces. Instruments function as first-class mediators between users and objects of interest.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction: An Interaction Model for Designing Post-WIMP User Interfaces
Beaudouin-Lafon 2022 TOCHI / Generative Theories of Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should expose domain objects (nodes, edges, queries) as directly manipulable entities mediated by interaction instruments, avoiding hierarchical menu structures that occlude the domain.

concepts.definition: The process of transforming abstract concepts or commands into first-class interactive objects that can be directly manipulated, visualized, and reused within an interface.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should reify abstract query concepts, transformation rules, and workflow steps as visible first-class objects users can edit and manipulate directly, not bury them in dialogs.

concepts.definition: The property enabling a single command to be applicable to objects of different types, maintaining a small command vocabulary while increasing interface power as reification adds object types.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support polymorphic operations (e.g., delete, copy, group) across heterogeneous node and edge types to prevent explosion of specialized commands.

concepts.definition: Making previously-provided user input or system output accessible for later use, enabling both input reuse (repeating action sequences) and output reuse (manipulating prior results).
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should enable users to capture and replay interaction sequences, clone subgraphs, and save/parametrize common workflows as reusable patterns.

concepts.definition: Three core principles for interaction: (1) continuous representation of objects of interest on-screen, (2) physical actions on objects rather than complex syntax, (3) fast, incremental, reversible operations with immediately apparent effects.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: Definition and Principles
Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must keep graph structure visible without occlusion by chrome, allow dragging/clicking nodes rather than menu navigation, and show incremental results of user actions.

concepts.definition: Principle that objects of interest should remain visible on-screen at all times, preventing the need for constant navigation, dialog switching, or memory-dependent interaction.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation
Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's graph visualization must persist as the primary canvas; secondary objects (layers, styles, metadata) should be visible as persistent panels, not modal dialogs.

concepts.definition: Interaction paradigms that extend or replace WIMP (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointing) conventions by leveraging new interaction techniques such as gesture, tangible objects, embodied interaction, and direct manipulation.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
Jacob et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should move beyond traditional menu-driven design, supporting touch gestures, pen input, multi-touch, and node-graph-native affordances.

concepts.definition: The objects of primary interest within an application domain that users actively manipulate to achieve tasks, as opposed to interface chrome elements.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's domain objects are nodes, edges, subgraphs, and queries; UI must prioritize these over menus, dialogs, and decorative elements.

concepts.definition: Tools or interface affordances that mediate user actions on domain objects, similar to physical tools (pens, hammers) that extend human capabilities in the real world.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should expose interaction instruments as reifiable objects: selection tools, layout tools, query builders, and filter instruments that are discoverable and composable.

concepts.definition: Extension of instrumental interaction principles to AI-augmented systems where prompts are embodied as reifiable interface objects supporting reflection (multiple interpretations) and grounding (instantiation from examples).
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments: Embodying Prompts as Instruments to Abstract & Reflect Graphical Interface Commands as General-Purpose Tools
concepts.implication: MetroGraph can leverage AI to generate query instruments from natural language prompts, with visual reflection showing multiple interpretations and grounding allowing users to refine from examples.

concepts.definition: In AI-augmented systems, the process of capturing ambiguous user intent as a reusable, directly-manipulable interaction instrument that can be edited and refined iteratively.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should allow users to capture intent (e.g., 'show high-degree nodes') as reifiable query instruments, editable and composable without returning to text prompts.

concepts.definition: In AI-augmented interaction, the design principle of presenting multiple interpretations of ambiguous user intent and multiple AI-model responses, enabling users to understand system behavior and refine intent.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should show multiple query interpretations or layout options generated by AI, allowing users to pick, compare, and blend results rather than accepting a single output.

concepts.definition: In AI-augmented systems, the principle of instantiating an AI-generated instrument from concrete examples, results, or extrapolations directly from the user's work context.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should allow users to create query instruments by selecting example nodes/edges, dragging result patterns, or modifying existing queries rather than writing syntax.

concepts.definition: Framework combining text-based instructions (prompts) with direct GUI interactions (brushing, clicking, dragging) to reduce ambiguity and improve precision in human-AI communication.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction: Modeling the Synergy of Prompts and Interactions in Human-GenAI Collaboration
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should accept both text descriptions and visual interactions (node selections, drag paths) together to ground user intent, addressing the ambiguity of text-only RAG/agent systems.

concepts.definition: Interaction paradigm where users communicate intent via natural language text prompts to AI systems, trading explicitness for intuitiveness but introducing ambiguity.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction
concepts.implication: While MetroGraph's strength is visual interaction, prompt-based queries should be an alternative channel for users familiar with text-driven workflows, augmented with visual feedback.

concepts.definition: Properties of an object or interface that suggest to a user how it can be used; distinguished between real affordances (physical properties) and perceived affordances (visual/cultural signals).
key_refs: Norman 1988 / Affordances and Design - Norman's Framework
concepts.implication: MetroGraph nodes should have clear visual affordances (e.g., drag handles for movement, hover states for interaction) signaling their manipulability without relying on explanatory text.

concepts.definition: Property of interaction where operations can be undone or reverted without permanent consequences, reducing user anxiety and encouraging exploration.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation
Bitterli et al. 2023 CHI / Point of no Undo: Irreversible Interactions as a Design Strategy
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must support full undo/redo for all manipulation actions, with clear visual history; destructive operations should be reversible until explicitly committed.

concepts.definition: User's internal representation of how a system works; effective interfaces align designer's conceptual model with user's mental model through consistent affordances and feedback.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / Mental Models in Interaction Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's node-edge graph metaphor must be consistent with how users conceptualize databases and queries; operations must behave predictably according to graph theory principles.

concepts.definition: Theory that cognitive processes are grounded in the body's interactions with the world, suggesting that physical/spatial interactions in interfaces engage cognition more effectively than abstract operations.
key_refs: Goldin-Meadow 2011 TOCHI / Embodied Cognition and the Magical Future of Interaction Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should leverage spatial layout and physical metaphors (dragging, proximity, containment) rather than menu hierarchies, since graph exploration is inherently spatial.

concepts.definition: Framework for post-WIMP interfaces built on four themes: naive physics (object behavior), body awareness (user awareness of their own actions), environmental context, and social awareness.
key_refs: Jacob et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should leverage naive physics (nodes fall, repel, cluster) and body awareness (drag/drop gestures) rather than abstract menu operations, making interaction feel intuitive.

concepts.definition: Formal framework for grounding HCI theories in natural/social science principles and translating them into actionable design principles; moves beyond descriptive theories to prescriptive guidance.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2022 TOCHI / Generative Theories of Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph design should be grounded in cognitive load theory, information foraging theory, and graph cognition research, not just UI conventions.

concepts.definition: Theory of how users seek and navigate information in systems, modeled on animal foraging behavior; users make decisions based on scent cues and effort predictions.
key_refs: Pirolli 2007 / Information Foraging Theory: Adaptive Interaction with Information
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should provide strong information scent (visual cues indicating navigation paths) and minimize effort to discover nodes/relationships, reducing cognitive foraging costs.

concepts.definition: The amount of working memory demanded by a task; interaction design should minimize extraneous cognitive load (e.g., UI navigation, syntax) to preserve capacity for domain tasks.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive Load Theory
Moran et al. 2024 / Cognitive Costs in Motor-Cognitive Performance Assessment
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must minimize chrome, menu depth, and syntactic burden; spatial layout and direct manipulation reduce cognitive load compared to command-line query languages.

concepts.definition: Motor control principle predicting interaction time based on target size and distance: T = a + b*log2(D/S+1), where D is distance and S is target size; guides optimal UI element placement.
key_refs: MacKenzie 1992 / Fitts' Law as a Research and Design Tool in Human-Computer Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should place frequently-used interaction targets (pan, zoom, select) close together and make them large; avoid requiring precise small clicks for common operations.

concepts.definition: Post-WIMP interaction paradigm using meaningful hand or body movements (swipes, pinches, rotations) to communicate intent, leveraging embodied cognition and reducing reliance on menus.
key_refs: Buxton 1990 / Gesture-Based Interaction
Wobbrock & Myers 2006 TEI / Tangible Meets Gestural
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support multi-touch gestures (pinch-to-zoom, two-finger pan, rotation) and pen gestures for annotation, not rely solely on mouse+keyboard.

concepts.definition: Design strategies for reducing or managing inherent ambiguity in user intent, especially in natural language or gesture-based systems, through clarification, feedback, and multimodal confirmation.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should resolve ambiguity in user queries through visual feedback, multiple interpretations, and reflection principles, not require users to rephrase until the system guesses correctly.

concepts.definition: In interaction design, the principle of partially applying functions/commands with some arguments preset, allowing subsequent arguments to be provided in context or interactively.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
concepts.implication: MetroGraph query builders could support curried commands where users select nodes first, then apply filters/transformations, rather than specifying all parameters upfront.
